## Overview

This weekly is review. Nothing in it is new. It puts the last few weeks together on one dataset: requests, reading structure, unnesting and hoisting, strings and regex, and joins.

The World Bank has a free API with data on every country in the world. You're going to answer a question that sounds simple:

**Which countries had the most people in 2023, and how is the world's population split up by region and income?**

On the way, you'll find out that "every country in the world" isn't quite what the World Bank sends you.

A few things:

1.  Add `#| echo: false` to your code blocks.
2.  Use a new block when you move to a new task.
3.  Code goes in the blocks. **Answers go outside them**, as prose. A comment inside a code chunk is not an answer.
4.  Save each raw response to a file **once**, then work from the file. After it's saved, add `#| eval: false` to the block that sends the request.
5.  Look at nested data one level at a time: `str(x, max.level = 1)`. Never print a whole response.

Due \[date\] at 8pm.

# Part 1: Ask

## Read the documentation first

The World Bank's documentation for building a request is here: <https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/898581-api-basic-call-structures>

> What format does the API send back if you don't ask for one? How do you ask for JSON?

> How many results do you get per page if you don't say? How do you ask for more?

## Make the request

Population has the indicator code `SP.POP.TOTL`. The endpoint for one indicator, for every country, is:

`https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL`

Build a request with `httr2` for **2023 only**, in **JSON**. Don't set the number per page yet. Look at it with `req_dry_run()`, then send it.

```{r}
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(httr2)
library(jsonlite)

Pop_raw <- "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL"

Pop_initial <- request(Pop_raw) |>
  req_url_query(
    date = 2023,
    format = "json"
  )
Pop_initial
req_dry_run(Pop_initial)
Pop_initial <- req_perform(Pop_initial)
resp_status(Pop_initial)


```

> What status did you get?
>
> 200 its working

Now look at the first element of what came back.

```{r}
#| warning: false

Pop_body <- resp_body_json(Pop_initial)
str(Pop_body[[1]], max.level = 1)
length(Pop_body[[2]])

```

> How many records exist in total? How many did you get? Is a 200 enough to know you got everything?
>
> 50 records exist in total. 200 is good to know that it works but It doesnt explain if we have everything we need

## Get all of it, and save it

Fix the request so you get every record in one response. Save it to `data/raw/wb_population_2023.json`, then read it back with `jsonlite::read_json()`.

```{r}
#| warning: false

pop_all <- request("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL") |>
  req_url_query(
    date = 2023,
    format = "json",
    per_page = 300
  )

pop_all <- req_perform(pop_all, path = "data/raw/wb_population_2023.json")
resp_status(pop_all)

```

```{r}
#| warning: false

data_pop_raw <- jsonlite::read_json("data/raw/wb_population_2023.json")
str(data_pop_raw[[1]], max.level = 1)
length(data_pop_raw[[2]])

```

> Fill this in:
>
> - URL: <https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL>
> - Date and time requested: Oct 25 26' 7:27pm
> - Status: 200
> - Records returned / records that exist: 266
> - One default that would have caught you:

# Part 2: Read the structure

```{r}
#| warning: false

str(data_pop_raw, max.level = 1)
str(data_pop_raw[[1]], max.level = 1)

```

> Look at the top level with `str(..., max.level = 1)`. How many parts are there? Do they have names? Is the top level a `{ }` or a `[ ]`? How do you know?

> Which part holds the pagination information, and which holds the data? How would you get to each one in R?

Now look at **one** record, one level deep.

```{r}
#| warning: false

str(data_pop_raw[[2]][[1]], max.level = 1)
str(data_pop_raw[[2]][[1]]$country, max.level = 1)

```

> Which fields are single values? Which are `{ }` with their own parts inside? What's inside `country`?

# Part 3: Make it a table

Create a tibble called `pop` with one row per record and these columns:

- `iso3` (`countryiso3code`)
- `country` (the country's name, inside `country`)
- `year` (`date`)
- `population` (`value`)

```{r}
#| warning: false

pop <- tibble(record = data_pop_raw[[2]]) |>
  hoist(
    record,
    iso3 = "countryiso3code",
    country = list("country", "value"),
    year = "date",
    population = "value"
  )
pop

pop |> 
  filter(is.na(population))

```

> Did you use `unnest_wider()`, `hoist()`, or both? Why that choice?

> How many rows? Does it match the total from Part 1? What is one row?
>
> 266 rows, one row is the population of a country in the year 2023

> Are any populations `NA`? Which places? What was the value in the raw JSON?
>
> Not classified has an NA value.

> Is `population` a number? Is `year`? Should they be?
>
> Population is a number year is just a value

# Part 4: Are these all countries?

Look through the `country` column.

```{r}
#| warning: false

pop |> 
  slice_head(n = 50)

pop |> 
  filter(is.na(iso3))

pop |> filter(iso3 == "")

```

> Name five rows that are not countries. What are they?
>
> Euro Area
>
> Arab World
>
> European Union
>
> Low income
>
> Other small states
>
> They are generalizations of clusters of different countries and regions put together.

> How many rows have an empty `iso3`? Are they `NA` or something else? How did you check?
>
> There is no rows that have NA values in iso3. I used filter is.na to check for NA values. the empty rows are displayed as empty strings

A classmate tries to remove the non-countries with a regex. Find every name that contains `"income"`, `"&"`, or `"and"`.

```{r}
#| warning: false

pop |> 
  filter(str_detect(country, "income|&|and"))

pop |> 
  filter(!str_detect(country, "income|&|and"))

pop |> 
  filter(!str_detect(country, "income|&|and|World|only|Union|area|members|demographic|developed|poor|blend|total|small|classified|Small"))

```

> Did that catch every non-country? Did it catch any real countries by mistake? Name them.
>
> I didnt get all of every non country it still has the IDA catagories.

> Improve the pattern as much as you can. Can a pattern ever do this job reliably? Why or why not?
>
> The pattern can be improved a lot by negating certain phrases but it will never be perfect.

# Part 5: Connect a second table

The World Bank also has an endpoint that describes each place: `https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country`. Request **all** of them in JSON, save the response, and read it back.

```{r}
#| warning: false

WB <- request("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country") |> 
  req_url_query(
    format = "json",
    per_page = 350
  )
WB_countries <- req_perform(WB, path = "data/raw/wb_countries.json")
resp_status(WB_countries)
wb_countries_raw <- jsonlite::read_json("data/raw/wb_countries.json")
str(wb_countries_raw[[1]], max.level = 1)
length(wb_countries_raw[[2]])


```

> How many places are in this table? Is that the same number as in `pop`? Why might they differ?
>
> There are 296 in this table

Create a tibble called `places` with `iso3` (`id`), `region` (inside `region`), and `income` (inside `incomeLevel`).

```{r}
#| warning: false

places <- tibble(place = wb_countries_raw[[2]]) |>
  hoist(
    place,
    iso3 = "id",
    region = list("region", "value"),
    income = list("incomeLevel", "value")
  ) |>
  select(-place)
places
  

```

> Try to keep only the places in Latin America & Caribbean with `filter(region == "Latin America & Caribbean")`. How many rows do you get? Now look very closely at the text of each region name (hint: `str_length()`). What's going on, and how do you fix it?
>
> You get 8 rows. We are still getting some other countries along latin america and the carribean

```{r}
#| warning: false

places |> 
  filter(region == "Latin America & Caribbean")
places |> 
  distinct(region) |> 
  mutate(len = str_length(region))

places <- places |>
  mutate(
    region = str_trim(region),
    income = str_trim(income))
    
places

places |> 
  filter(region == "Latin America & Caribbean")

```

## Mutating join

Add `region` and `income` to `pop`.

```{r}
#| warning: false

pop_joined <- pop |>
  left_join(places, join_by(iso3))
nrow(pop_joined)

pop_joined |> 
  filter(is.na(region))

            

```

> Which key did you join on? Why not the country name, or the two-letter id inside `country`?
>
> I joined by iso3 because both tibbles shared that column

> How many rows before and after the join? Should it change?
>
> It has 266 rows

> Which rows got `NA` for `region`? Why didn't they match?
>
> The countries that are listed by income have NA values.

## Filtering joins

In `places`, the non-countries have `region` equal to `"Aggregates"`.

Make a table of only the real countries in `pop`, using a filtering join. Then make a table of everything you threw out.

```{r}
#| warning: false

real_places <- places |>
  filter(region != "Aggregates")
nrow(real_places)
pop_countries <- pop |>
  semi_join(real_places, join_by(iso3))
pop_thrown_out <- pop |>
  anti_join(real_places, join_by(iso3))
nrow(pop_countries)
nrow(pop_thrown_out)
pop_thrown_out

```

> How many countries? How many places did you throw out? Does anything in the thrown-out list surprise you?
>
> there are 217 countries and we threw out 49. Nothing really suprises me it just threw all the generalized countries and commbined regions

> Compare this to your regex in Part 4. Which would you trust, and why?
>
> I would trust these joins more than the regex because these joins filter by actual countries and not by gerneralizations

# Part 6: Answer the question

```{r}
#| warning: false

countries_clean <- pop_joined |>
  filter(region != "Aggregates", !is.na(region))

countries_clean |>
  slice_max(population, n = 5)

pop_by_region <- countries_clean |>
  summarize(
    total_pop = sum(population, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = "region"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_pop))
pop_by_region

pop_by_region |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_pop, y = fct_reorder(region, total_pop))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "World Population by Region (2023)",
    x = "Total Population",
    y = "Region"
  )
```

> What were the five most populous countries in 2023?
>
> India, China, U.S, Indonesia, Pakistan

> What is the total population by region? By income level? Make one of these a plot.

> The data includes a row called "World." Compare its population to the sum of your real countries. Are they the same? Why might they not be?

> If you had **not** removed the aggregates, what would your regional totals have been? How wrong, and in which direction?

# Bringing it together

A classmate's project uses World Bank data. They downloaded a table, summed a column, and wrote "the world's population is tens of billions of people."

Write them a short note, roughly 200 words, that:

When first importing the raw World Bank data it includes each country and then it also includes a some generalizations and combinations of different countries. It contains aggregates such as East Asia, High Income and World. If you summed the raw population from the World Bank data it would give you the tens of billions of people because it includes these generalizations. In the world today there are 196 countries and the raw data gives you 296. You could use slice to see these. Using a join is better than using str detect because it can join dataset by common columns to bind together actual countries.

- explains what probably went wrong
- tells them how to check for it
- tells them how to fix it, and why a join is safer than a pattern
- names one default in the API that could have caught them
